en: Title: Buddhakapālatantra Source: Luo 2010 (chapters 9–14) Input: PDSz, Budapest 2025.iii.22
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the chapter on conduct, which is very difficult to obtain, by means of which a yogin performs all forms of conduct with an exceedingly excellent woman. 9.1
Endowed with the eight accomplishments, one should thereafter commence the conduct;
whatever beings seek as their accomplishment, that very thing one should always grant them. 9.2
Holding a skull-cup in his hand, the practitioner wanders on his course of conduct;
having become naked with disheveled hair, he goes wherever and whenever he pleases.
In this manner, the course of conduct must always be performed. 9.3

Completely liberated from all obscurations and having attained equality with space, the wise one wanders for alms from house to house, free from doubt. Taking whatever is agreeable to the mind, he dwells in meditation, beyond all uncertainty. 9.4
When the yogi seeks alms with a joyful mind, he should cultivate the realization that "no" is the very nature of emptiness. (9.5)
That which is "Jā" is the unsurpassed vehicle; it is called Mahāmudrā.
By merely hearing "Jāha," the yogi becomes devoted to the Dharma. (9.6)
Afterwards, one should consume the substance placed upon the skull;
by the mere consumption of that substance, the high-minded one falls and falls into a deep sleep.
Whether in the house, in the courtyard, on a heap of chaff, or at the foot of a tree;
wherever, whenever, and by whatever means—with a joyful mind—such a one who is engaged in the yoga of conduct will certainly attain Mahāmudrā. (9.8)
And so it is said in the Tantra:
"In whatever way, by whatever means, and through whatever [circumstances], one becomes a Buddha; when all conceptual constructions have been destroyed, everything is pure by its very nature. (9.9)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, on Conduct, in the *Buddhakapāla-tantra*, the unsurpassed *Yoginī* tantra, which is more secret than the most secret.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim this definitive chapter on gold, which is certain and solely for the benefit of sentient beings. 10.1
Pearls, mother-of-pearl, royal silk, and coral—
by means of these, beings become wealthy when the teacher is pleased. (10.2)
It has been stated that this medicine is not external— it is neither bark nor sprouts,
nor is it mercury (pārada).
Neither sulphur nor mica, nor magnetite, antimony, nor copper— nor indeed any other metal— is the supreme perfected medicine. 10.3
Having heard such words, the mighty Vajrapāṇi prostrated at her feet; with firm devotion toward the Being alone, he said, "Excellent, O Goddess! (10.4)
What are those divine medicinal herbs, and of what nature would their accomplishment be?
Tell me, O Great Goddess; I wish to hear this with reverence. (10.5)
Speak, O Great Goddess!
Which are those excellent perfected medicinal herbs? By what means do sentient beings, intent on increasing their lifespan, become possessed of wealth? (10.6)
Which great medicinal herbs are perfected merely by being recited and do not require prior service (*pūrvasevā*)? By what substance do many [women] become fruitful, as if they were mothers of sons?
Having died, he returns to life; he does not die again and again.
He said:
"While staying right here in this house, the great medicinal herbs are perfected."
And though that divine, excellent vessel is perfected, the foolish, being deluded, do not know it. || 10.8 ||
Fools are shrouded by ignorance and are solely intent on their own self-interest; how can they accomplish the welfare of sentient beings? Alas, alas! They are devoted only to misery. (10.9)
It abides as the essence within a beautiful vessel,
hidden within the pericarp;
it is the channel named Rasanī situated in the center.
The divine great medicinal herbs remain.
Just as there exists a supreme great medicinal herb by means of which even an immeasurable amount of iron attains the state of gold with a single application,
so too does the tongue [attain its power]. || 10.11 ||
The supreme medicinal herb is perfected by means of a preliminary preparation of combinations;
I shall now declare those combinations here—let them listen with firm devotion. (10.12)
When a woman possesses the *sūryavatī* [sign], is in her youth, dark-complexioned, and learned in this tantra, [she is a suitable consort]. (10.13)
She should be shameless, indifferent, free from greed, and affectionate toward living beings;
she should serve the Tathāgatas constantly, remain well-concealed, and be merciless. 10.14
Having taken hold of this woman, one should employ the divine great medicine for a man of excessive passion;
he whose movement becomes too rapid does not achieve success. 10.15
Such is this great medicinal herb, exceedingly difficult to find even for the Buddhas; a wise man should cultivate that woman whose mind is utterly heroic. 10.16
And so it has been said:
"The perfected ones proclaim that fortitude is indeed the supreme state of a leader."
Therefore, indeed, one with a heroic mind should cause [the offering] to be placed in a beautiful vessel. 10.17.
In that regard, a woman named Sūryavatī, who is exceedingly rare even for a goldsmith,
should contemplate the moon within her own heart as being smeared with the essence of the perfected elixir (siddharasa).
In that regard, the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* is preceded by the single substance of all things and adorned by the King of Mountains (*merurāja*). || 10.18 ||
Thereafter, the wise one, solely intent on the welfare of sentient beings, should begin the ritual activity;
he should place the substance in a fine vessel, with his left hand bent toward the right.
One should place a round noose made of copper together with iron;
or, in its absence, even just iron alone.
Thereafter, the wise one should commence the ritual action with a mind characterized by heroic yoga; having become liquefied through the seed-syllable king of Sumeru-candra, he is beyond doubt. 10.21
It rests within a beautiful vessel; from that state of transition, the wise one should quickly take up the divine [substance] and smear it with molasses, even if it is somewhat coarse. 10.22.
Having coated it with a mere amount of molasses, one should cast it into the midst of fire; thereafter, the wise man protects it, and it undoubtedly becomes gold. || 10.23 ||
In a single month, he pierces a hundred palas;
such is the divine method of gold-making,
difficult to find even throughout the three worlds.
If the great medicine is immeasurable,
then the Buddha, too, is immeasurable.
This, O Great King, is the tantra.
Whatever object is described, all of them attain reality through the yoga of the Buddha-Kapāla. || 10.25 ||
The wise one who possesses learning and great intelligence, yet performs this immeasurable [offense], all of them go to hell for as long as they do not encounter Buddhas. 10.26
The eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma are unsurpassed for yoginīs;
all those [teachings] become false merely through the failure of the medicinal herbs.
Even those beings who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution and who have harmed the Buddha and the Dharma,
shall attain accomplishment through this divine great medicine.
If this is so even for one free from doubt at that very moment, how much more so for one who is devoted to meditative cultivation and solely intent on the welfare of sentient beings? (10.28)
The most excellent medicinal herbs are accomplished;
even gold and silver are produced.
A person lives for ten million eons, until the very attainment of the Buddha-knowledge. 10.29
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the means for barren women to obtain sons;
by merely bathing together [with this], she shall instantly become possessed of a son.
I shall proclaim the procedure for bathing as it was taught by the former leaders:
having prepared colored powders of five hues, or indeed white alone,
one should fashion a formidable maṇḍala that causes terror to the seizing spirits.
There, one should place four jars; they should be round with large bellies. The wise man should fill them with water and also wrap them with cloth. 10.32.
The mark should be written with one's own blood;
it must be that of a woman who is barren.
Having taken the primary element [blood], [one should proceed].
The wise one should smear the mouth of the jar. || 10.33 ||
Thereafter, for one devoted to meditative cultivation, abiding in the state of Śrī Heruka—
[who is] intensely terrible, black and red, born from the Vajra-hūṃkāra,
terrifying like the fire of universal destruction, and possessing a formidable hūṃkāra.
They know this as its pronunciation. 10.34.
The wise one should meditate upon [the deity] with four arms and one face, thus knowing the recitation; he should visualize him dancing within the vase, most terrifying. 10.35.
Behind them followed four men of great renown, bearing swords,
with minds filled with extreme rage.
By merely bathing at that moment, those men, though terrifyingly formidable,
are struck by the sword in the sky and slain.
For one thus engaged in yoga, a woman who has been bathed likewise becomes possessed of a son,
even if she is barren, through the yoga of the Buddha-Kāpāla.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, the ritual procedure for bathing those who are barren with divine great medicinal herbs, in the *Buddhakapāla-tantra*, the unsurpassed [tantra] of the Yoginīs, which is more secret than the secret.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the chapter concerning the yoga of Garuḍa.
A wise man should draw the mandala according to the previously stated procedure.
The wise one should manifest Heruka, surrounded on all sides by the eight yoginīs;
with the previously mentioned symbols, arms, and so forth, his supreme color is indeed white.
The yoginīs of the cardinal directions are white, while those of the intermediate directions are red. (11.2)
And by means of the previously mentioned rites, the wise one establishes the mandala;
he should draw four vases and the previously mentioned symbols.

Thereafter, one should favor the disciple through the application of the method for becoming a Vidyādhara. According to the previous ritual procedure, there is the formal request, the giving [of initiation], and the feast circle (gaṇacakra). 11.4
Afterwards, one should cause the mandala to be worshipped;
with this very mantra, one should again bestow grace upon the disciple. || 11.5 ||
Once bitten on the ground, nothing can be brought back to life;
they say that one who has been bitten by Time is abandoned by the snake-charmer.
Thereafter, the wise one, a yogin of the Buddha-Kāpālin, should commence the ritual action;
having become Heruka himself, surrounded on all sides by the eight yoginīs,
they are all white-bodied.
But [he should practice] yoga according to the rule. || 11.7 ||
Having taken flour made from śāli rice, one should fashion two vidyādharas;
with extreme concentration, one should place a sword in their hands. 11.8.
One should write the mantra on his heart, or likewise on any leaf;
having prepared ink with mahātaila, the wise one should write the mantra.

The mantra: Oṃ buddhakapālinī hrīḥ! Oṃ kāpālavajriṇī āḥ! Destroy all nāgas! Raise up the vidyādharas! Revive those bitten by the god of death! O, O Blessed One, Buddhakapālinī, the destroyer of all nāgas! Haḥ ha haḥ svāhā! This is the heart-mantra of the vidyādhara. 11.10.
Having thus completed [the ritual], one should place the leaf upon the heart;
with this mantra, one should invoke [the deity] seven times using a sprout. || 11.11 ||
Oṃ buddhakāpālinī | ghaṭ ghaṭ ghaḍa ghaḍa hrīḥ hrīḥ haḥ haḥ he he haṃ haḥ || 11.12 ||
Merely by reciting it seven times, two Vidyādharas appear in the sky and fight;
one of them falls, broken into pieces.
There is no doubt that one has been bitten by a snake. || 11.13 ||
There is another [reason] for the instrument:
those [items] such as the lotus-stand and so forth, which are difficult to obtain,
are not written in the manuscript— [namely] fifteen [of them].
It is understood through the grace of the Guru. || 11.14 ||

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the Determination of the Instruction on the Means for Becoming a Vidyādhara, in the *Buddhakapālatantra*, the Supreme Yoga of the Yoginīs, which is more secret than the most secret.
Then Vajrapāṇi and the yoginī Citrasenā, having prostrated themselves again and again, spoke thus: || 12.1 ||
Excellent, O Queen, highly wise and preeminent yoginī!
You have spoken of a practice that is difficult to find even throughout the three worlds. (12.2)
I have seen all the tantras and those practices which are very difficult to obtain;
yet that which has been spoken by you in this tantra has not been taught by all the Buddhas.
Oh, how truly devoted she is to the welfare of sentient beings!
Oh, how truly the mother of all Buddhas!
Oh, how truly devoted she is to the Mahāmudrā! 12.4
Speak, O Goddess, of all those applications of mantras which are very difficult to obtain,
by which yogins perform various wonders and manifold marvels.
O Goddess, tell me the practical application of whatever was stated in the first chapter.
Having heard such words, the yoginī Citrasenā let out a loud,
boisterous laugh,
and all the gods were terrified.
All the Māras flee in terror and all obstacles come to an end;
it is a marvel that all the supreme Jinas have declared this to be the certainty of laughter. 12.7
He said:
"Having taken hold of the raised banner,
he also takes the meat from it."
Having taken the bone from the region of his waist, one should have a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) constructed.
Taking his skull-bowl, one should cause a wick to be placed with that very head;
one should fill it with its oil and set it upon the sacrificial pit. || 12.9 ||
Another [person] should also apply collyrium;
as long as the collyrium falls,
the yogin, having become a bearer of the Buddha-kapāla, [should remain].
Uttering this mantra: || 12.10 ||

Oṃ! O Buddhakapālinī, hold, hold, hold, hold; cause to be held, cause to be held; dry up, dry up; burn, burn; drāṃ drāṃ; āṃ māṃ sāṃ ra vāṃ; perform, perform! O Blessed One, do not transgress the command of Buddhakapāla! Quickly, fall, fall, cause to fall, cause to fall! Oṃ oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Subjugate! O Blessed One, hūṃ srāṃ phaṭ! || 12.11 ||
Such is the power of this king of mantras that it can even wither the three worlds;
[it subdues] bhūtas, vetālas, ḍākinīs, rākṣasas, piśācas, and the like. 12.12
Upon merely hearing it, they go to dissolution;
so too do all other obstacles.
One should recite the mantra for that long.
Until the soot falls off. || 12.13 ||
As soon as it has fallen into the collyrium,
the highly wise yogi should take hold of it with both hands and then drink Kelimālinī again. 12.14.
A yogi who is solely intent on the welfare of sentient beings should desire a sixteen-year-old girl who is endowed with beauty, youth, and grace. (12.15)
Having become naked with the topknot loosened,
the wise one should utter the mantra *hāḥ hoḥ*;
then Kelimālinī should cause [the disciple] to drink, and thereafter the play should commence.
Becoming one who laughs with loud, repeated laughter, the Great Compassionate One should place the highly divine collyrium in her left hand while uttering the *phetkāra* sound.
Thereafter, the wise one should gradually perform the application with ritual actions;
he should take the substance produced from that, which arises from the filaments of a lotus.
With that very same collyrium, one should apply it to the ring finger and the thumb;
then one should cause a flower to be offered and have pills prepared, numbering one hundred and eight.
Having consecrated each individual pill with one hundred and eight recitations of the mantra, one should chant:
oṃ buddhakāpālinī hrīḥ hūṃ phaṭ || 12.20 ||
O mighty-armed one, by means of this mantra, collyrium is obtained that is difficult to find even in the three worlds;
it is difficult to find in all tantras, and it is the supreme [secret] of the yoginīs.
By merely applying collyrium with the ring finger and the thumb,
one beholds all the Buddhas, as numerous as the atoms in the three-thousandfold world system.
Eight million yojanas;
he sees both below and above with merely the touch of his left hand.
At that very moment, he becomes auspicious. || 12.23 ||
Merely by anointing the forefinger, one beholds the world of the moving and the unmoving, as well as the spirits of the departed, ghosts, and demons, and other perfected beings.
One sees for a thousand million yojanas both below and above;
by merely rubbing it with the left hand,
one becomes healthy, of this there is no doubt.
Merely by anointing with the middle [ingredient],
one becomes a performer of the most extraordinary wonders;
[one appears] seven palm trees in height, with a crest of black flames.
This collyrium is difficult to obtain; it causes all clouds to burst asunder.
Merely by being rubbed with the left hand, they attain human form at that very moment;
and merely by being applied with the thumb of the Great-Souled One, it becomes collyrium.
But as for images, lingas, mountains, trees, and whatever others there may be—
by the mere glance of his wrathful eye, they are shattered into a thousand fragments.
Furthermore, by merely rubbing [the eyes] with the left [hand], one becomes healthy; of this there is no doubt.
By merely applying collyrium with the little finger and the thumb, one becomes invisible to the eye at that very moment.
It is not seen even by the Buddhas. || 12.29 ||

The wise man may wander among the thirty-three gods and take whatever object he desires, even the most precious goods from their treasuries; yet at that very moment, the high-souled Kajjala seizes it all away. 12.30.
Such is this collyrium practice, exceedingly difficult to obtain through various methods;
by the mere application of this ointment, he effects a transformation of his own form.
By this very collyrium,
one becomes a Vidyādhara. [One may also become] a crow, an owl, a bird, a snake, a dog, a jackal, a great tiger, a bear, or a hyena.
Likewise flies, and likewise elephants and donkeys. || 12.32 ||
In this way, one creates various forms with soot;
indeed, everything can be done everywhere.
However, the practical application of this is extremely difficult to master.
The practical applications (prayoga) not written in the book are to be understood through the grace of the Guru. || 12.33 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the yoga that is exceedingly difficult to attain;
through the union with the bones of the mantra, it performs various wonders.
Oṃ buddhakāpālinī hrīṃ hraṃ. This practice involving an elephant bone is to be performed as the ritual application for killing. 12.35.
Oṃ buddhakāpālinī khaṃ hrīṃ phaṭ! With a horse bone, one should perform the very difficult rite of eradication. || 12.36 ||
Oṃ buddhakāpālinī tryāṃ hrīṃ hrīḥ!
One should perform the piercing of the enemy's heart with a cow bone. || 12.37 ||
Oṃ buddhakāpālinī āḥ hūṃ phaṭ. The great wise one should perform the rite of immobilization using a dog's bone. 12.38.
Oṃ buddhakāpālinī hrīḥ vauṣaṭ. Attraction is to be performed with human bone. 12.39.
Oṃ buddhakāpālinī vuṃ hūṃ!
One should perform the rite of delusion using the bone of a donkey. 12.40.
Oṃ buddhakāpālinī āṃ hrīḥ hrīḥ.
Subjugation should be performed with an owl bone. 12.41.
Oṃ buddhakāpālinī hāḥ phaṭ hūṃ.
Enmity [is achieved] by means of a stake made from the bone of a bird. 12.42.
Oṃ buddhakāpālinī jriṇī drāṃ!
By means of the bone of a donkey, there is the paralyzing [of enemies]. || 12.43 ||
Oṃ buddhakāpālinī dhara 2 hā he ho haṃ haḥ | By means of a jackal’s bone, victory in battle is attained. || 12.44 ||

Oṃ buddhakāpālinī rama 2 krīḍa 2 haṃ haḥ | With the bone of a buffalo, a twelve-year-old girl plays in amorous sport; whether by night or by day, the man’s mind does not fall [into distraction]. 12.45.
Oṃ buddhakāpālinī taṭa 2 trāṭaya 2 maṭ sphaṭ sphoṭaya utpāṭaya hūṃ phaṭ! With a snake’s bone, one uproots trees. 12.46.
Oṃ sukapālinī ghara 2 maṭa 2 trāṭaya 2 paṭa 2 praṭāpaya 2 truṭa sphaṭa moṭaya 2 saṃkrāmaya hrīṃ hūṃ tryāṃ phaṭ.
By means of a tiger’s bone, mountains are uprooted. 12.47.
Oṃ buddhakāpālinī he! Terrify! Slay! Ghuṭa ghuṭinī! Strike the hearts of all forest plants! Disperse them! Rama 2! Terrify 2! O Bhagavatī! Aṃ āṃ āṃ taṭ 2 hūṃ phaṭ!
With this, forest plants are warded off. (12.48)
He said:
Whatever is contemplated upon that stainless mirror of the singular mind, that too falls [within it].
The all-knowing ones know everything; nevertheless, they are grasped through conceptualization. 12.49
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, on the application of various mantras, in the *Buddhakapālatantra*, the unsurpassed *Yoginī* tantra, which is more secret than the most secret.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the pure chapter on purification, which is difficult to obtain.
A sister, a niece, a mother, a daughter, and even a wife—a wise man should desire them in this way, for such is what is required for the Mahāmudrā. 13.2
The Ḍombinī, the Nartakī, the Dhoriṇī, the Caṇḍālinī, and the Carmakāriṇī are remembered [as the five]; thus the wise man should desire these five excellent Yoginīs.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain [the method] for purifying the impure mind.
The sister would be the eye, and the co-wife indeed the ear;
the mother would be the sense of smell, and the daughter the sense of taste;
the wife would be the mind.
These five excellent divine [mantras] bestow the Mahāmudrā. || 13.5 ||
Delusion arises from the *nartakī*, and hatred from the *ḍombinīs*; passion arises from the *dhūrvī*, and pride is known to arise from the *caṇḍālinī*.
Maherṣyā and Carmakārī—these five were excellent women.

Through the eye, delusion is seen; through sound, even hatred arises. Through the nose, one experiences passion; likewise, taste gives rise to pride. Through touch, envy is born, as well as the impurity of the mind. (13.7)
Therefore, O one of great wisdom, for a yogi whose mind is intensely absorbed in yoga,
there shall be no attainment [in this life]; rather, through purity, it will come to pass in another birth.
How can there be existence through non-existence? What kind of existence would that be? How could non-existence become an existence to be cultivated? || 13.9 ||
"Sister, how is it that one with a pure mind will not see such a form—whether fair, dark, or born of a black complexion? (13.10)
"Sister, how is it that sound is heard, and resonance is indeed of three kinds?
One whose mind is pure and who is thus engaged in yoga does not hear such things. (13.11)
Having observed that the nose is of three kinds, who is that most secret mother?
Since the mind is unperceived, how can even passion arise? 13.12

With their own tongues they enjoy substances possessing the six flavors; such is the nature of taste. Through that taste they experience what is joined with it; what then is the nature of the form? 13.13
Through the mind there is pleasure and even joy; the mind experiences pleasure from the investigation of both. Yet, in that [state], no investigation exists. 13.14
In existence there is no non-existence, and non-existence is likewise [not found] in existence;
the emptiness of both existence and non-existence—these are the purity of the mind. 13.15
Hereafter, I shall explain the purification of the external body.
Compassion and loving-kindness would be associated with [wrong] views, as would the embrace.
When the yogic self is well-guarded and the excellent woman is likewise joyful,
that union of both is known by me as the moment of equanimity, whose essence is the aesthetic flavor (rasa).
How can one who is thus engaged in the yoga of such contemplation be afflicted by passion?
Suffering arises from seeing; embracing yields a slight result of that;
from friction joy arises; and from the remainder of it all, dejection follows. (13.18)
Thus, joy and dejection arising within the three realms are the fruit of this;
one whose self is united with the perfectly pure mind is not afflicted by the three things.
Whatever food and drink there may be, as well as any meal that brings pleasure,
the knower of yoga should always regard all of it as feces, urine, and so forth.

Whatever pleasure-play there may be, including embracing and kissing, as well as rubbing and massaging—that is called the Mahāmudrā. For one who contemplates in this manner, success is attained; of this there is no doubt. (13.21)
The five yoginīs are the bestowers of the great mudrā of the Buddha’s splendor;
the yogi should worship them with desire and is not defiled thereby. 13.22
One who is joined with the ointment of non-attachment is not afflicted by its defects;
that yogi is not smeared by the defects of worldly existence, for he has reached the supreme reality. (13.23)
As long as the sense-objects are not uprooted,
how can there be the body of a wise one?
It is like a fresh sprout on a thorn bush.
Just as there is no excellence in a tree [without fruit]. || 13.24 ||
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, on the Purification of the Mind, in the *Buddhakapāla-tantra*, the *Yoginī-niruttara*, which is more secret than the most secret.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the chapter on the praise of Citrasenā. 14.1.
Likewise:

Then the Bodhisattvas, headed by Vajrapāṇi, and the Yoginīs, equal in number to the atoms of Mount Sumeru—with eyes wide open and hearts thrilled—Citrasenā and the others, prostrated themselves and offered praise. (14.2)
Oh, how wonderful is the Blessed Goddess!
She is the mother of all Buddhas, Lakṣmī, the formidable one of great renown, who is affectionate toward the welfare of sentient beings. 14.3
The Goddess is possessed of great compassion; she is Great Wisdom, the Great Seal, and the bestower of the fruit of the great purpose. 14.4
In the *Buddhakāpāla-mahātantra*, those things which have not been revealed by the Buddhas,
but were guarded by Vajradhara himself and were beyond the range of the Bodhisattvas—
those the Goddess spoke, making them manifest with a single sound. (14.5)
Oh, how truly great is this Goddess, who embodies the essence of all yoginīs!
That which she has accomplished is exceedingly difficult to attain;
it is beyond the reach of all other Tathāgatas.
Once that goddess has been made manifest, she is accomplished merely by reciting [this].
Aho! May the Blessed Ladies listen! May the Yoginīs and Bodhisattvas listen!
May those free from passion and possessed of great supernatural powers listen!
May the Tathāgatas and all the Buddhas listen, as well as the Nāgas, together with gods and humans. || 14.7 ||

May they rejoice in all the merit that arises from the mere recitation of this king of tantras; may they dedicate it for the sake of Mahāmudrā and offer it to those who are mines of the qualities of a Buddha. 14.8
May they forgive me for having revealed the hidden meaning,
the mantras, the extremely difficult applications,
and the well-guarded domain.
Having made [this teaching] manifest for the sake of sentient beings, may the supreme Victors forgive me. || 14.9 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the recitation of the mantra of great power;
if one desires excellent and divine accomplishment,
one should recite it through the yoga of the Buddha-Kapāla.
Oṃ hrīṃ buddha hūṃ kāpālinī āḥ.
At entry: Oṃ; at departure: Hrīṃ; at rest: Buddhaḥ; in happiness: Hūṃ; at sunset: Kāpālinī; at rising: Āḥ. 14.11.
Such a recitation is very difficult to obtain;
through such a yoga of the Buddha-Kapālin, and with such a recitation joined with pride (*māna*), accomplishment (*siddhi*) occurs without a doubt. || 14.12 ||
The heart mantra:
Oṃ buddhakāpālinī āḥ hūḥ haiḥ hūṃ phaṭ. || 14.13 ||
The subsidiary heart mantra (upahṛdaya-mantra): oṃ buddhakāpālinavajriṇi hau durjaya durlakṣe hūṃ phaṭ || 14.14 ||
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the procedure for the time of consecration (seka), by which means a disciple of firm devotion requests the Wisdom Consort (prajñā). 14.15
Having prepared the fivefold mandala with fragrant substances,
the Great Goddess, adorned by all the Buddhas, makes her request.
He causes [the disciple] to drink divine substances and places edible food in his mouth;
having drunk the substance, his mind becomes joyful and delighted.
The goddess, filled with joy upon seeing him, spoke these words:
"I am mired in the mud of saṃsāra; O beautiful one, be my savior! (14.18)
O Goddess of great renown and compassion, please bring to rest those conceptual constructions that are frequently joined with latent predispositions. 14.19
One should first offer all those ornaments, adorned with every kind of jewelry;
afterwards,
the wise one, with a mind of firm devotion, should offer oneself.
One should present various kinds of food and various kinds of drink before him, by whom wisdom has been satisfied and who has been honored by all the Buddhas. (14.21)
Remaining right here are the Buddhas and other leaders of the Siddhas;
likewise, all the Ḍākinīs and others who belong to the family of compassion abide in that very place. (14.22)
O friend, that state where even one's own nature has perished and nothing remains is clearly the gateway to supreme bliss; ask this of the feet of the Guru. 14.23
Homage to him, by whose arising the sense faculties simultaneously set along with their objects;
he who alone possesses a form as beautiful as that of the Conqueror Abhinanda.
Some [principle] remains vigilantly hidden within the hearts of the wise.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, on the Recitation, Mudrās, Entreaty, and the Introduction to All Tantras, in the *Buddhakāpālatantra*, the *Yoginīniruttara*, which is more secret than the most secret.
Thus spoke Citrasenā, the Yoginī, and all the other Yoginīs; and Vajrapāṇi and all the other Bodhisattvas, as well as all the Mahābodhisattvas, each remaining in their own place, became silent.
Thus ends the *Paramarahasya* (The Supreme Secret) in the *Buddhakapālatantra*, according to the system of the Mahāyoginīs. [Vajrapāṇi°] corrected; the edition reads *vajraprāṇi*.
